classification.difficultyReason: Divide an annual quantity into weekly shares and then into seven equal personal shares.

content.prompt: Fran’s family want to make their 689 Easter eggs last for one year.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How many Easter eggs can they eat per week?

answer.worked:
Use $52$ weeks in one year.
$$\begin{align*}689\div52&=\frac{689}{52}\\689\div52&=\frac{53}{4}\\689\div52&=13\frac{1}{4}\end{align*}$$
The family can eat $13\frac{1}{4}$ Easter eggs per week.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If there are 7 people in Fran’s family, how many Easter eggs will one person eat per week if the eggs are shared equally?

answer.short: $1\frac{25}{28}$ Easter eggs per person per week.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}13\frac{1}{4}\div7&=\frac{53}{4}\div7\\13\frac{1}{4}\div7&=\frac{53}{4}\times\frac{1}{7}\\13\frac{1}{4}\div7&=\frac{53}{28}\\13\frac{1}{4}\div7&=1\frac{25}{28}\end{align*}$$
Each person can eat $1\frac{25}{28}$ Easter eggs per week.

teachingContext.methodNote: Divide into equal weekly quantities, then divide the mixed-number weekly quantity by seven using its improper-fraction form.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Both parts share the annual egg quantity; part b uses the weekly result of part a and remains in the same question.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Teacher 9a gives 13 1/4 and 9b gives 1 25/28. The source annual total 689 divided by 52 gives 53/4 eggs weekly, and dividing that quantity among the source seven people gives 53/28 eggs each weekly. Both labelled entries agree.

Front stalls: $\frac{1}{4}\times1080=270$ people.

The added oil represents the unfilled $\frac{2}{5}$ of the capacity.

content.prompt:

answer.worked:
The fraction scored on day 5 is
$$\begin{align*}
f_5 &= 1-\left(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{5}+\frac{7}{32}\right)\\
&=1-\left(\frac{80}{480}+\frac{96}{480}+\frac{192}{480}+\frac{105}{480}\right)\\
&=1-\frac{473}{480}\\
&=\frac{7}{480}.
\end{align*}$$
Let $x$ be the total number of runs.
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{7}{480}x &=21\\
x &=21\times\frac{480}{7}\\
&=1440.
\end{align*}$$
The daily totals are
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Day 1} &=\frac{1}{6}\times1440=240\text{ runs}\\
\text{Day 2} &=\frac{1}{5}\times1440=288\text{ runs}\\
\text{Day 3} &=\frac{2}{5}\times1440=576\text{ runs}\\
\text{Day 4} &=\frac{7}{32}\times1440=315\text{ runs}\\
\text{Day 5} &=21\text{ runs}.

content.prompt: A train from Alston to Brampton stops at two intermediate stations. At the first of these, $\frac{1}{2}$ of the train’s passengers leave and 135 new passengers board. At the second station, $\frac{1}{3}$ of the passengers who arrived on the train at the first station leave, and 110 new passengers board. The train arrives at Brampton with 350 passengers. How many passengers were on the train when it left Alston?

answer.short:
630 passengers.

Both departure fractions refer to the passengers originally on the train.
answer.worked:
The passengers who arrived at the first station are the original passengers. Both departure fractions therefore refer to that same group. The new passengers remain on board.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Original fraction remaining}&=1-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}\\\text{Original fraction remaining}&=\frac{6}{6}-\frac{3}{6}-\frac{2}{6}\\\text{Original fraction remaining}&=\frac{1}{6}\\\text{New passengers}&=135+110\\\text{New passengers}&=245\\\text{Original passengers remaining}&=350-245\\\text{Original passengers remaining}&=105\\\text{Original passenger total}&=105\div\frac{1}{6}\\\text{Original passenger total}&=105\times6\\\text{Original passenger total}&=630\end{align*}$$

Check: 315 original passengers leave at the first station and 210 at the second. The final passenger count is $630-315+135-210+110=350$.

entries.description: How do we multiply two fractions such as \(\frac23\times\frac34\)? We will use the area model for multiplication that we used in Chapter 1. Begin with a square of side length 1. Its area will also be 1. Now divide the square into rectangles by drawing vertical lines and horizontal lines, as shown. Thus, we divide the height into quarters and the base into thirds. Each rectangle has area \(\frac1{12}\). Next, shade the rectangle with side lengths \(\frac23\) and \(\frac34\), as shown in the diagram. We can see that the shaded region is made up of \(2\times3=6\) rectangles, each of area \(\frac1{12}\), so the area of the shaded region is the product of the sides, \(\frac23\times\frac34\). But this is also equal to 6 lots of \(\frac1{12}=\frac6{12}\). We conclude that: \(\frac23\times\frac34=\frac6{12}\).
